title: Dynamic degradation policies for tenant-aware load shedding, rate limits, and circuit breakers
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Summary: Implement a dynamic degradation framework that composes priority queues, tenant-aware admission control, adaptive rate-limits, and multi-stage circuit breakers. The goal is to preserve critical SLOs for high-priority customers and graceful-degradation semantics for lower-priority traffic during overloads and partial regional outages. This ticket covers design decisions, runtime policy format, rollout plan, observability, and a verification plan for canarying policy changes.
background: We currently use a mix of static admission control knobs and kernel-level shedding that treats all traffic uniformly. Incidents in Q4 showed that a single overloaded region can cause global tail latency regressions because low-priority background workloads consumed burst capacity. We need a unified policy layer that is SLO-aware and region-aware, enforces tenant budgets, and supports staged degradation (e.g., disable embeddings batching -> degrade QoS -> reject low-priority requests).
goals: Introduce policy objects that express per-tenant and per-route priorities, SLAs, and degradation actions
Support admission control decisions that use real-time SLO signals (latency p95/p99, available GPU QPS) and tenant budgets
Implement multi-stage circuit breakers (soft->hard) with automatic cool-off and regional isolation behaviors
Provide observability: dashboards, alerts, and per-tenant shedding metrics for post-incident analysis
Deploy with canarying and shadow-testing to validate correctness without impacting customers
non_goals: Replacing existing network-level rate limits or authentication policies
Rewriting the serving runtime — this is a policy/orchestration layer that coordinates with the runtime via well-defined hooks
approach: We will add a policy evaluation layer in the request ingress path. The layer will consult: (a) static priority from tenant config, (b) tokenized runtime SLO view (computed per-model, per-region), (c) tenant burn-rate vs budget, and (d) current circuit-breaker state. The evaluation yields one of: ACCEPT, ENQUEUE (priority queue), GRACEFUL_DEGRADE (apply cheaper execution: forced quantized model/shortened context/response sampling), or REJECT. Enqueue will feed into a continuous batching queue with eviction based on priority and latency budget. Circuit breakers are implemented with multi-threshold triggers: suboptimal (soft) threshold causes degradation actions; critical (hard) threshold drops low-priority requests and trips a breaker, isolating the region or model variant. Policy objects are authored as versioned YAML and reconciled by the control plane. Runtime hooks are exposed as gRPC endpoints for fast local decisions and as a fallback central evaluator for config changes.
design_decisions: Use a two-tier decision model: fast-path local evaluator in each serving node (cached policies) + central policy store for config changes
Policy format is declarative YAML with fields: priority, slo_targets, budget_window, degrade_actions, breaker_thresholds. We will version as v1alpha and migrate iteratively
Admission control will consult a lightweight SLO proxy that emits rolling p50/p95/p99 and estimated available token QPS per node
Graceful degradation modes are ordered and composable: RATE_LIMIT -> BATCH_PRUNING -> MODEL_VARIANT -> TRUNCATE_RESPONSE -> REJECT
Circuit breaker cool-off will use exponential backoff with jitter and a minimum closed-window to avoid flapping
work_items: Console: per-tenant shedding dashboard and simulator (ENG-9274-03)
Integration: runtime changes to accept degrade hints (ENG-9274-04)
E2E: shadow testing harness + canary rollout (ENG-9274-05)
Docs + runbook: incident playbooks and operator guide (ENG-9274-06)
acceptance_criteria: Policy schema implemented and validated by unit tests
Local evaluator returns admission decision within 200 microseconds p95 under load
Graceful_degrade action exercised in shadow mode and verified to reduce GPU work by >= 40% for targeted requests
Circuit breaker transitions observed in staging with defined soft/hard thresholds and cool-off behaviour
Dashboard shows per-tenant reject/enqueue/degrade metrics and burn-rate; alerts fire when tenant burn-rate > budget for 3 consecutive windows
Canary rollout completes without customer-visible SLA violations for high-priority tenants
risks: Incorrect priority ranking could unfairly throttle paying customers — mitigation: require manual review for tenant priority changes and a 24h shadow phase
Policy mismatch across nodes could lead to inconsistent behavior — mitigation: strong config version pinning and fast reconciliation with health checks
Too-aggressive degradation may reduce model quality — mitigation: implement degrade actions with telemetry to track quality and automatic rollback on regression
Increased decision latency in ingress path — mitigation: optimize evaluator and provide bypass for requests that are pre-authorized with guaranteed capacity
test_plan: Unit tests for policy parsing and evaluator, integration tests simulating high-QPS regions with per-tenant traffic mixes, staging chaos test that kills regional capacity to verify regional isolation and cross-region failover. Run shadow policies for 48 hours on a subset of customers before enabling active enforcement. Load test to validate 200 microsecond decision latency p95.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge schema + evaluator to staging; 2) Enable shadow evaluation for 10% of traffic (7 days); 3) Enable active enforcement for low-priority traffic only in a single non-critical region (72 hours); 4) Expand enforcement and add canary for high-priority tenants using manual approval; 5) Full rollout with automated monitoring and automated rollback criteria
observability: Expose metrics: policy_eval_latency_ms, decisions{accept,enq,degrade,reject}, per_tenant_degrade_rate, per_tenant_reject_rate, breaker_state, available_qps_estimate. Dashboards: tenant burn-rate, global burdened regions, degradation action effectiveness. Alerts: sustained p99 latency increase after policy change, per-tenant burn-rate spike, unexpected breaker flapping.
